slides.title: Language variation: who speaks how, where, when
slides.body:
**Sociolinguistics**: study of variation in language by speaker + community + situation. Founded by William Labov (1927-2024) + others 1960s-70s.

**Variation dimensions**:
• **Geographical (dialect)**: regional accents + words. American English: Boston, Texas, NYC, Pittsburgh.
• **Social (sociolect)**: class, ethnicity, age. African American Vernacular English (AAVE) vs General American.
• **Situational (register)**: formal vs informal vs intimate vs technical.
• **Individual (idiolect)**: every speaker has unique combo.
• **Historical (diachrony)**: language change over time.

**Variables + variants**:
- (ing): walking vs walkin' (different realizations of same variable).
- (r): rhotic (Midwest, General American) vs non-rhotic (Boston, NYC, British RP, AAVE).
- Lexical: 'soda' vs 'pop' vs 'coke' (regional in US).
- Grammatical: 'I'm walking' vs 'I be walking' (AAVE habitual be).

**Variation correlates with**:
- Social class + education.
- Ethnicity + race.
- Gender (often subtle).
- Age (apparent-time hypothesis = real-time change).
- Style + topic.
- Setting + audience.

**Labov's NYC Department Store study (1962)**: variable (r) in 'fourth floor.' Asked clerks at Saks (high-class), Macy's (middle), Klein's (low). Rhoticity (pronouncing /r/) higher at Saks; lower at Klein's. Quantified social stratification of a single variable.

**Classic findings**:
- Curvilinear principle: middle classes lead in vernacular variants.
- Female speakers often lead change-from-below (Labov 2001).
- Adolescents drive sound change; ~80 yr per generation cycle.
- Network density: tight networks resist change; weak ties spread.

slides.title: Standard, prestige, + linguistic discrimination
slides.body:
**Standard language**: socially-prescribed variety; usually associated with educated + powerful speakers. Standard American English, Received Pronunciation, Putonghua (Mandarin), Modern Standard Arabic.

**Origins of standards**: historical accident + power. Standard French = Île-de-France dialect. Standard Italian = Tuscan (Dante). Standard German = Luther's Bible + Saxon chancery. Mandarin Putonghua = 1950s Beijing-area standardization.

**Prescriptive vs descriptive grammar**:
- Prescriptive: rules of 'correct' usage. Strunk + White; AP/MLA style. Often invented or arbitrary.
- Descriptive: actual usage patterns. Modern linguistics.

**Common prescriptive 'rules' linguistics rejects**:
- 'Never split infinitives' (Latin-inspired; English fine to do so).
- 'Never end sentence with preposition' (English does; 'a feat up with which I shall not put' is awkward).
- 'Singular they' is grammatical + ancient.
- 'Ain't', 'gonna', 'wanna' are not 'incorrect' — different register.

**Linguistic discrimination + prejudice**:
- Speakers judged by speech (Lippi-Green 1997 'English with an Accent').
- AAVE speakers underemployed + misjudged in education (Rickford + King 2016 on Rachel Jeantel testimony).
- 'Foreign accents' affect hiring, housing, credibility.
- Educational tracking sometimes based on dialect.
- Standardization can suppress minority varieties.

**Code-switching**: shift between varieties within conversation. Strategic: matched to interlocutor, topic, audience.

**AAVE (African American Vernacular English)**:
- Rule-governed variety with specific syntactic + phonological features.
- Habitual 'be' (he be working = he works regularly).
- Copula deletion (he tall, she busy).
- Existential 'it's' (it's a man at the door = there's).
- Negative concord (ain't nobody got time).
- Stigmatized in education but linguistically full + valid system.
- Origins: creolization + English contact; debate.

Oakland Ebonics resolution (1996): AAVE recognized as legitimate. Backlash + clarification followed.

slides.title: Language change + the apparent-time hypothesis
slides.body:
**Language change** happens continuously + observably:
- Phonological (/r/ loss in non-rhotic; vowel shifts).
- Lexical (new words: 'rizz', 'cap', 'no cap'; old words shift: 'gay', 'awful' once = awesome).
- Grammatical ('whom' declining; like-quotative spread; double modals in some varieties).
- Pragmatic (politeness conventions shifting).

**Mechanisms**:
- **Sound change**: gradual or abrupt; chain shifts (Great Vowel Shift, Northern Cities Shift).
- **Lexical change**: word coinage, borrowing, semantic shift.
- **Grammatical change**: grammaticalization (V → AUX → affix), reanalysis.
- **Pragmatic change**: politeness drift; address-term evolution.

**Apparent-time hypothesis**: synchronic differences between age groups reflect diachronic change in progress. If 20-yo speakers use feature X at 80% but 60-yo speakers at 20%, X is in change.

**Sound change in progress**:
- Northern Cities Shift (Midwest US): /æ/, /a/, /ɔ/, /ʌ/, /ɛ/, /ɪ/ rotate.
- California Shift: similar rotation.
- /uw/ fronting in much of US ('boot' shifted from back to mid).
- Vocal fry + 'uptalk' (rising final intonation) — generational + gender-related.

**Lexical innovation**:
- Slang lifecycle: in-group → mainstream → quaint. Cycles ~5-15 years.
- 'On fleek', 'lit', 'savage', 'sus' all peaked + waned.
- TikTok + social media accelerate spread; Gen Alpha innovations (rizz, gyat, skibidi) viral globally.

**Grammatical change**:
- 'Like' quotative ('he was like, ...'): originating ~1980s; now standard for narrative quotation.
- Singular 'they': always existed; explicit gender-neutral use spreading 2010s+.
- 'Going to' → 'gonna' → 'gon' grammaticalization.

**Death + revitalization**:
- ~40% of world's ~7000 languages endangered.
- Welsh, Hebrew, Hawaiian, Maori, Cornish: successful + ongoing revitalizations.
- UNESCO + Endangered Languages Project + community efforts.

**Pidgins + creoles**:
- Pidgin: simplified contact language; nobody's L1; restricted use.
- Creole: pidgin acquires native speakers; full language emerges. Haitian, Tok Pisin, Hawaiian Pidgin, Sranan.
- Creole genesis is hot debate: superstrate-driven, substrate-driven, bioprogram (Bickerton).

question.question: Apply Labov's variationist method to a sociolinguistic study
question.goal: Design a study to investigate how speakers in your community use the (-ing) variable (walking vs walkin').

steps.reveal: **Dependent variable**: % realization of word-final -ing as alveolar [n] (walkin') vs velar [ŋ] (walking). Per speaker + per token.

acceptedAnswers: age, gender, class, education, ethnicity, style

steps.reveal:
**Independent variables**: 
- Age (young vs older).
- Gender.
- Social class (income, education, occupation).
- Ethnicity / regional background.
- Speech style (casual interview vs reading passage vs minimal pairs — 'classic Labov 5 styles').
- Topic (emotional vs neutral).
**Sample**: stratified random sample. ~40-60 speakers spanning demographics. Recruit via personal network + community events.

**Sociolinguistic interview**: 1-2 hr per speaker. Topics elicit casual speech (childhood, emotional events); then reading passage (more formal); then minimal pairs (most formal). 'Observer's paradox' = speakers self-monitor when observed; use 'attention to speech' modules to elicit unmonitored vernacular.

steps.prompt: Analysis: how to detect significant patterns?

acceptedAnswers: multivariate regression with VARBRUL or mixed-effects logistic

steps.reveal:
**Analysis**: code each (-ing) token as [n] or [ŋ]. Mixed-effects logistic regression with social predictors + style + speaker (random effect). Or VARBRUL (specialized tool for this). Patterns: typically -in' favored by male + lower-class + casual speech; -ing by formal/female/upper-class.

This design pattern (Labov-style sociolinguistic interview + regression) has produced thousands of studies revealing systematic patterns across English, French, Spanish, German, etc.

question.question: Classify each feature as STANDARD or NON-STANDARD English (descriptively, no judgment).

items.label: 'To boldly go where no one has gone before'

question.explanation:
Standard vs non-standard (descriptive, no prescriptive judgment):
• **Standard**: features acceptable in published/edited written English + formal speech. Includes: split infinitives (now accepted), preposition stranding (always natural English), singular 'they', subjunctive 'were.'
• **Non-standard**: features marked by region, class, ethnicity, or rare in standard. Negative concord ('ain't got no'), AAVE habitual 'be', regional pronouns (y'all, yinz), regional 'anymore' (= 'these days') in positive sentences.

Non-standard ≠ wrong. AAVE, regional dialects, Pittsburghese — all rule-governed systems. 'Y'all' fills genuine gap (English needs 2nd-person plural pronoun). Linguistic discrimination judges speakers by these markers; descriptively, they're features. Some 'rules' linguists reject: 'don't split infinitives', 'don't end with preposition' — both fine in modern English.

question.question: Why was Labov's NYC Department Store study (1962) foundational for sociolinguistics?
options: First rigorous quantitative demonstration that linguistic variation (rhoticity in 'fourth floor') correlates with social stratification + style-shifting. Sampled 3 stores at different status levels (Saks, Macy's, Klein's) + asked clerks 'where are the women's shoes?' eliciting 'fourth floor'; coded /r/ as present/absent. Showed: higher-status store → more rhoticity; emphatic repetition → more rhoticity (style-shift toward prestige). Replicated since hundreds of times across languages + variables. Established variationist methodology as core of modern sociolinguistics.
question.explanation:
**Labov's NYC Department Store study (1962)** — foundational sociolinguistic methodology:

*Background*:
In 1960s NYC, /r/ in postvocalic position ('fourth' [fɔɹθ] vs [fɔθ]) was variable. Earlier (1900s): NYC mostly non-rhotic (like Boston, RP). Pressure from outside (rhotic varieties became prestigious) was shifting NYC toward rhoticity.

*Design*:
- 3 department stores selected by social-class hierarchy:
  - **Saks Fifth Avenue** (upper-middle): high-prestige.
  - **Macy's** (middle): middle.
  - **S. Klein** (lower-class): lower.
- Labov visited each store + asked clerks for items on the fourth floor.
- Forced response: 'fourth floor' — contains two opportunities for /r/.
- First response (casual); then repetition asked ('excuse me?') → more emphatic style.
- ~265 employees sampled.

*Coding + analysis*:
- /r/ realization: present, absent, intermediate.
- Per store × first vs emphatic response.

*Results*:
1. **Social stratification**: Saks > Macy's > Klein's in /r/ presence.
2. **Style-shift**: emphatic > casual in /r/ presence. Speakers shifted toward prestige variant when more attentive.
3. **Real-time confirmation**: subsequent decades + repeats showed continued rhoticization of NYC.

*Why it was revolutionary*:

1. **Quantitative + replicable**: Labov coded tokens by ear; replicable by anyone with method. Prior sociolinguistics + dialect-geography descriptive only.

2. **Social factors as predictors**: rather than treating variation as 'noise,' showed it systematically tracks social structure.

3. **Style-shifting**: showed speakers + listeners are aware of variable + use it socially.

4. **Change-in-progress**: predicted continued change based on age-stratified observation — apparent-time hypothesis.

5. **Pragmatic methodology**: real-world setting (department store) + minimal interference. Subsequent studies use sociolinguistic interview, ethnography, computer-mediated.

*Subsequent work*:

- **Martha's Vineyard study** (Labov 1963): centralized diphthongs ([aɪ] → [əi]) used to mark identity by year-round residents resisting tourism.
- **NYC vowel system + Lower East Side** (Labov 1966): systematic class + style-shifting + change-in-progress.
- **Norwich /h/-dropping** (Trudgill 1974): UK extension; gender + class patterns.
- **Detroit AAVE** (Wolfram 1969): documented systematic AAVE features.
- **Atlas of North American English** (Labov + Ash + Boberg 2006): dialect map of vowel shifts.
- **Variation + change in many languages**: extension worldwide.

*Theoretical implications*:

1. **Variation is systematic**: linguistic + social factors structure it.
2. **Variation is functional**: speakers use it for identity, power, solidarity.
3. **Variation drives change**: bigger changes emerge from accumulated variation.
4. **Variation challenges idealization**: native speakers don't have static homogeneous grammar.

*Tools + methods that grew from this*:

- **VARBRUL** (Pintzuk + Sankoff): statistical software for variable rules.
- **Mixed-effects logistic regression** (Rbrul, lme4): modern statistical analysis.
- **Ethnographic + community-of-practice** approaches (Eckert): smaller, more contextual.
- **Corpus sociolinguistics**: large corpora + computer analysis.
- **Social media + variation**: Twitter, Reddit + dialect studies.

*Continued influence*:
Variationist sociolinguistics is one of the few subfields where every published paper traces lineage back to Labov 1962. Methodology unchanged in essence + extended to: digital communication, multilingualism, identity construction, perceptual + acoustic analysis.

Labov passed in 2024 + is widely considered the most influential sociolinguist of the 20th century.

slides.workedSolution: Labov 1962 NYC: studied /r/ realization in 'fourth floor' at Saks/Macy's/Klein's. Showed social stratification (high-class store → more rhoticity) + style-shifting (emphatic repetition → more rhoticity). First rigorous quantitative sociolinguistic study; established variationist methodology. Replicated worldwide; extended to: NYC vowels, Detroit AAVE, Atlas of North American English. Theoretical: variation systematic + functional + drives change. Modern: VARBRUL, mixed-effects regression, ethnographic. Labov passed 2024; foundational figure.

question.question: Drag to the approximate percentage of the world's ~7000 languages classified as endangered or threatened.
question.explanation: UNESCO + Endangered Languages Project: ~40-50% of ~7000 living languages endangered (definitely + severely + critically endangered). ~700+ languages have <100 speakers. Loss rate: ~1 language every 2 weeks. Major endangered: many Indigenous Americas, Australian Aboriginal, African micro-languages, Pacific. Revitalization successes: Hebrew (extinct 2000 yr, revived 19th-20th c.), Welsh (English pressure but stable), Maori (NZ official; +50% speakers since 1990s), Hawaiian.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why linguistics distinguishes descriptive from prescriptive grammar + the consequences for education + policy.
question.rubric: Mentions: descriptive grammar = what speakers actually say (linguist's data). Prescriptive = what speakers 'should' say (style guides, schoolbooks). Linguistics is empirical descriptive science. Prescriptive rules often historically arbitrary: 'don't split infinitives' (Latin-inspired), 'don't end with preposition' (Latin-inspired), 'singular they' (always existed in English). Many features prescriptively stigmatized are part of valid varieties: AAVE habitual 'be', double negatives, regional pronouns. Consequences of conflating: linguistic discrimination — judging speakers, employment, education, legal credibility by dialect/accent. Lippi-Green 'English with an Accent' documents extensive bias. Educational reform: AAVE + dialect-aware teaching reduces achievement gap; Oakland Ebonics resolution (1996) was misunderstood as 'teaching bad English' but was about recognizing students' L1 to teach Standard English bidialectalism. Modern linguistics + education increasingly value linguistic diversity + bidialectal/multilingual competence. Closes: prescriptive ≠ correct; descriptive ≠ permissive; linguistic education builds awareness + reduces discrimination.
